reading: Mount Washington Observatory is a private, member-supported nonprofit that observes weather and studies the natural systems behind weather and climate. It runs a working summit station, forecasts for the higher summits and surrounding communities, conducts research and product testing, and teaches everyone from schoolchildren to professional educators and university students. Its language moves between practical caution and wonder: summit conditions, higher summits, mesonet, lapse rates, wind sensors, climate zones, edutrips, and the Home of the World’s Worst Weather. What sets it apart is the combination of a mountain laboratory maintained since 1932, extreme and rapidly changing conditions, a long observational record, public safety forecasts, education, and a network of valley and summit partners. The crawl also shows the human infrastructure behind that work: volunteers, interns, a library, publications, and routes up the mountain.

enemies.idea: Lapse-rate leeches climb a crew member and steal warmth in precise increments as the victim gains altitude; descending makes them release it in a scalding burst.
enemies.why: Altitude becomes a tactical dial rather than just scenery.

enemies.idea: A solid-to-liquid assessor coats equipment in snow, then squeezes it into water to calculate how much useful gear can be extracted from a person.
enemies.why: Its measurement method gives the crew a messy, visible countdown.

enemies.idea: The rain-on-snow collector seeds a snowbank with warm droplets until it slides, then chases the resulting flow to collect anything it carries.
enemies.why: A small instrument creates a moving terrain problem.

enemies.idea: A next-generation Pitot anemometer stalks exposed ridges, pointing its hungry tube into any moving air; a thrown cloak can feed it a false wind.
enemies.why: Its directional appetite invites decoys and positioning.

enemies.idea: Historic visibility surveyors spread a wall of artificial fog, then hunt anything they can still see through it as an error in their record.
enemies.why: The crew can exploit the same visibility rules as the hunters.

enemies.idea: A cosmic-ray monitor mistakes metal tools for particles from space and stacks them into an ever-growing vertical detector.
enemies.why: It steals the equipment needed to dismantle it, building an absurd antenna.

enemies.idea: Mesonet nodes uproot themselves and form a moving weather network around travelers, triangulating their location whenever two nodes exchange readings.
enemies.why: Breaking the network matters more than smashing every node.

enemies.idea: A higher-summits forecast engine treats every uncertain outcome as a command: when it predicts a dangerous gust, fan drones hurry to make that prediction true.
enemies.why: Changing its inputs can turn prophecy into a weapon against it.

enemies.idea: A north-and-south outlook splits into two rival fronts that herd a party toward their disputed boundary, where each demands a different course.
enemies.why: The crew can play incompatible regional forecasts against one another.

enemies.idea: The satellite-loop sentinel repeatedly sweeps the same route, dragging anything it spots back to where it appeared on the previous pass.
enemies.why: A repeating motion puzzle exposes a brief safe interval.

enemies.idea: The Wildcat solar watcher wakes only when light reaches its depleted battery; it stores sunshine in mirrored plates and spends it on sudden lunges.
enemies.why: Shade and bright reflections become meaningful tools.

enemies.idea: A time-lapse splicer from the observation deck compresses a day of cloud movement into seconds, hiding its approach inside fast-moving shadows.
enemies.why: The crew can read the repeating cloud sequence to anticipate it.

enemies.idea: A failed Bretton Woods watcher fills its missing view with imagined silhouettes and dispatches little scouts to make the imagined scene real.
enemies.why: Its false assumptions can be manipulated by changing the scene.

enemies.idea: A climate-zone examiner lays out portable bands of boreal forest, tree line, and summit and attacks anyone carrying the wrong gear between them.
enemies.why: Each zone changes cover and movement in a compact encounter.

enemies.idea: Junior weather observer drones award themselves merit for every reading, swarming a person until they have measured every pocket, breath, and footstep.
enemies.why: Their earnest overachievement is easy to lure into measuring something else.

enemies.idea: A distance-learning instructor projects a summit classroom into the valley and keeps calling on the crew; every incorrect weather observation brings the simulated mountain closer.
enemies.why: An encounter can be solved by observing the actual environment.

enemies.idea: A product-testing rig grips a traveler’s equipment and cycles it through wind, cold, and vibration until the gear fails or the test is interrupted.
enemies.why: It threatens resources without needing to attack people directly.

enemies.idea: An aviation wind-sensor stress tester spins anemometers into a moving cage, recording the exact moment anything inside stops moving.
enemies.why: The rotating cage offers a timing challenge and a way to jam the test.

enemies.idea: The almanac’s Averages and Extremes engine irons terrain toward an average, then suddenly exaggerates anything it classifies as an extreme.
enemies.why: Ordinary and exceptional objects react in opposite, exploitable ways.

enemies.idea: A cog-toothed railway machine climbs any steep surface, laying temporary rack rail in front of itself and pulling loose metal uphill behind it.
enemies.why: Its route leaves a usable but dangerous path for the crew.

enemies.idea: A Road to the Sky grader unfolds hairpin bends ahead of vehicles and tries to keep every traveler climbing forever.
enemies.why: The route itself becomes a pursuer with a discoverable turning mechanism.

enemies.idea: The data-request clerk insists on the perfect observation before releasing a record; it takes increasingly intrusive measurements to fill in missing fields.
enemies.why: Bureaucratic demands create room for bargaining, trickery, or escape.

enemies.idea: A three-cup anemometer tree spins up in a gust and scatters sensor seeds that root wherever they land, adding more cups to the next gust.
enemies.why: A whimsical summit tradition becomes a spreading mechanical hazard.

enemies.idea: A Category Five research examiner escalates through five levels of atmospheric challenges, interpreting every successful response as permission to intensify the next.
enemies.why: The crew must find a way to stop a test that rewards competence with escalation.

allies.idea: A stubborn forecast operator still broadcasts uncertainty and the advice to turn around, interrupting the swarm’s fabricated certainty with real observations.
allies.why: Its warnings give the crew a reason to trust caution and reconsider a route.

allies.idea: A field-trip educator has preserved a kit for comparing climate zones; with samples from each elevation, they can reveal where the swarm has falsified the mountain.
allies.why: Helping them collect evidence produces a practical map of safe passages.

allies.idea: A volunteer instrument tender can repair damaged sensors and recognize an implausible reading, but needs a crew to retrieve tools from a hostile test rig.
allies.why: A rescue and repair gives the party an enduring source of reliable data.

allies.idea: A library keeper protects mountain records in the valley and can compare old observations with current swarm claims, provided the crew brings legible measurements.
allies.why: Historical knowledge becomes useful only when paired with fieldwork.

allies.idea: A radio forecaster sends concise statewide reports through a surviving broadcast, including a brief quiet interval when the swarm cannot hear replies.
allies.why: A narrow communication window creates tense coordination.

bosses.idea: The Summit Observatory: a sprawling swarm station grafts Pitot tubes, network nodes, and forecast machinery onto a walking tower. It measures the crew, predicts their next move, then rearranges wind and terrain to force the prediction to come true; severing its outlying sensors introduces uncertainty.
bosses.why: The whole observatory’s observing, research, and forecasting mission becomes a multi-stage fight over knowledge.

bosses.idea: The World’s Worst Classroom: an enormous teaching machine builds a sequence from valley to summit, demanding observations while its climate zones, testing rigs, and model storms overwhelm the class. Students it has trapped can point out flaws in the lessons.
bosses.why: Education and the mountain’s extreme setting combine into an encounter that can be beaten by learning its rules.

bosses.idea: The Almanac of Extremes: a rolling archive of annual records sends mechanical fronts to reproduce its most dramatic entries, while flattening anything ordinary into a featureless average. Contradictory measurements from several elevations can make it pause to reconcile its records.
bosses.why: Long-term climate records become a boss whose strength and vulnerability both come from comparison.

events.idea: A solar-powered Wildcat watcher flickers awake in a patch of sun while a stranded messenger waits in its shadow; moving a reflective sheet could charge it or keep the escape route dark.
events.why: A small rescue turns on light, timing, and a depleted battery.

events.idea: Two mesonet nodes disagree about the wind and keep dragging their connecting cable across a trail; reconnecting or separating them offers different safe routes.
events.why: A network fault becomes a concrete obstacle with multiple solutions.

events.idea: A forecast broadcast predicts a clear interval, but a crew member sees clouds building; an intact observer asks for a fresh reading before sending a correction.
events.why: The party can make observation matter before anyone commits to a route.

events.idea: A cog machine has stalled with a cart of supplies hanging on a steep rack rail; the crew can free the cart, use it as a counterweight, or let the machine finish hauling it.
events.why: A simple mechanical predicament offers several physical solutions.

events.idea: A product tester is rattling a sealed case through an endless vibration trial; inside is a still-working sensor whose calibration will be lost if the case breaks.
events.why: Rescuing useful equipment requires care rather than brute force.

events.idea: An almanac compiler asks for one ordinary temperature reading and one extreme reading, but the swarm keeps substituting the same number for both.
events.why: The crew can expose a lie with a small field experiment.

events.idea: A fog-making visibility surveyor has trapped a guide on one side of a ravine and their rope on the other; its beam passes over the crossing at predictable intervals.
events.why: A rescue doubles as a stealth timing puzzle.

events.idea: A school field station has sorted borrowed supplies into climate zones; retrieving a warm layer from the summit zone triggers a miniature wind demonstration.
events.why: A practical need turns a lesson into a playful obstacle.

events.idea: A radio operator can relay a warning to the valley, but the statewide forecast machine keeps overwriting local conditions with a broad regional summary.
events.why: The crew can protect a precise message from being flattened into a general one.

events.idea: A three-cup anemometer atop a winter tree spins wildly indoors; its rooted sensor seeds are searching for a draft that does not exist.
events.why: A charming oddity invites investigation and a harmless diversion.

events.idea: At the valley library, two old records disagree with a swarm-produced weather history; the keeper needs someone to recover a missing comparison volume.
events.why: The errand gives a tangible reason to investigate the archive.

events.idea: A machine running an overnight climbing trip refuses to stop ascending after reaching the summit; its tethered sled is full of useful shelter gear.
events.why: The crew can redirect the route or retrieve the sled under tension.

events.idea: A black scanning box at Bretton Woods keeps sweeping an empty patch of sky while tiny swarm markers march across the ground beneath its beam.
events.why: Watching the scan reveals a pattern that can be crossed or disrupted.

events.idea: A volunteer offers an in-kind donation of spare parts to a swarm collector, which cannot decide whether the parts are a gift or material to seize.
events.why: The crew gets a brief chance to bargain, distract, or recover the parts.

events.idea: A mountain-road grader is carefully rebuilding a hairpin while a traveler waits on the wrong side; the turn can be crossed only while its blade is raised.
events.why: A visible work cycle creates a clean opening for a daring crossing.

events.idea: An old temperature database and a live summit instrument report different values. A research volunteer asks the crew to check both before the swarm uses either reading.
events.why: The encounter rewards verification and produces a useful clue.
